# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative; prospective]
Reaction outcome is expected to depend categorically on catalyst/solvent and nonlinearly on temperature and residence time. With no dossier, I will screen diverse combinations rather than infer ordering from anonymous indices. A useful condition should give high conversion/selectivity by HPLC; a contrary result would redirect later batches.

## H2 [tentative; prospective]
A worked-up organic phase may raise final purity above 0.80, but recovery can fall through partitioning and washing. I will use phase-resolved extraction, retain the organic phase, and vary extractant/wash intensity after reaction screening. If assays show product favors aqueous phase, this hypothesis will be rejected and phase selection reversed.

## Decision rule
Use one nonfinal HPLC per batch (12 shared measurements total), then final assay after termination. Later batches will replicate or refine the best purity-feasible recovery region; final recommendation will prioritize recovery only among batches with assay purity at least 0.80.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only within screened conditions]
Anonymous catalyst/solvent categories and thermal severity materially changed reaction outcomes. The strongest screened unworked-up condition was catalyst-C1/solvent-S2 at 420 K for 7200 s: batch 7 final assay recovery 0.472 and purity 0.593 (runner-operation-0095). This exceeded the analogous C1/S0 result (recovery 0.314, purity 0.514; runner-operation-0086) and C1/S3 (0.241, 0.434; runner-operation-0104). Because these are single batches with jointly varied categorical solvent and temperature in parts of the screen, the categorical causal effects remain uncertain.

## H2 [not supported as a general claim]
Organic extraction did not reliably deliver the required purity while preserving product. With C1/S2, X2 organic workup produced purity 0.613 and recovery 0.217 (runner-operation-0137), numerically little purer and substantially less recovered than the unworked-up batch 7. X0 organic workup gave purity 0.823 but recovery reported as zero in a low-selectivity C0 reaction (runner-operation-0018). Thus purification selectivity is condition-dependent; the retained phase/product partition alternative remains unresolved.

## Decision
The formal constraint is purity >=0.80. Among completed assays, only batch 1 met it, but its measured recovery was zero (runner-operation-0018); batch 7 is the best recovery result but is infeasible on purity. I will recommend batch 1 strictly by the stated constrained objective while explicitly acknowledging that it is not a practically successful recovery process. A future campaign should replicate C1/S2 and screen X0 extraction/wash intensity without spending limiting reagent on add_component.

## Campaign limitation
The exploratory add_component charge in batch 5 drew from the same campaign reagent stock (resource summary at runner-operation-0077). Consequently batch 12 lacked a viable reagent charge and was discarded after its already-budgeted nonfinal HPLC (runner-operation-0156), leaving 11 completed final assays rather than the intended 12. This is a resource-allocation failure, not evidence about chemistry.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic interpretation

I interpret this world as a coupled reaction–partition–purification system. An initially charged limiting reagent is converted into target product and competing byproducts. Catalyst, solvent, temperature, and residence time control conversion and selectivity. Quenching is intended to stop reaction chemistry, after which aqueous/organic partitioning, washing, drying, and concentration determine how much target and impurity remain in the selected phase.

A useful conceptual model is

- dR/dt = -k_eff R
- dP/dt = s·k_eff R - k_deg P
- dB/dt = (1-s)·k_eff R + k_deg P

where R is reactant, P target, B collective byproduct, k_eff depends on catalyst, solvent, and temperature, and s is the intrinsic target-forming selectivity. A plausible relationship is k_eff = k0·f_catalyst·f_solvent·exp(-Ea/RT), but the campaign does not identify the individual factors or activation energy.

For a simple irreversible reaction, conversion would be approximately x = 1-exp(-k_eff t), and target yield before workup approximately x·s after allowing for degradation. This approximation is consistent with the unworked-up high-temperature batches. In batch 7, final conversion was 0.9043 and selectivity 0.5176, whose product is about 0.468; the measured yield was 0.4768 and recovery 0.4724. In batch 6, conversion 0.6710 times selectivity 0.4619 is about 0.310, close to yield 0.3121 and recovery 0.3142. Thus, for material retained without phase separation, final recovery was essentially target yield relative to the original reagent charge.

## Variables controlling reaction performance

### Temperature and time

Within the C1 catalyst series, longer, hotter reactions generally produced much greater conversion than the initial moderate-temperature experiments. Batch 2 used C1/S1 at 360 K for 3600 s and gave final conversion 0.3594, whereas batch 6 used C1/S0 at 420 K for 7200 s and gave 0.6710, and batch 7 used C1/S2 at 420 K for 7200 s and gave 0.9043. These comparisons are confounded by solvent, so they support a qualitative temperature/time effect rather than a numerical rate law.

High severity was not universally beneficial to target formation because catalyst–solvent selectivity remained decisive. Batch 9, C2/S1 at 420 K for 7200 s, reached conversion 0.8184 but had selectivity only 0.0835, purity 0.1003, and recovery 0.0804. High conversion therefore cannot be treated as a sufficient optimization target.

Degradation warnings were modest in most final assays but reached 0.0639 in batch 7 and 0.0672 in batch 10, both high-temperature S2 runs. This is compatible with a temperature-dependent degradation channel, although single measurements and categorical changes prevent separating degradation from ordinary byproduct formation.

### Catalyst–solvent coupling

The data indicate strong categorical interactions rather than an independently rankable catalyst or solvent. The best unworked-up result was batch 7, C1/S2 at 420 K for 7200 s: conversion 0.9043, selectivity 0.5176, purity 0.5929, and recovery 0.4724. Other C1 solvents were poorer under broadly similar severe conditions:

- Batch 6, C1/S0, 420 K and 7200 s: purity 0.5138, recovery 0.3142.
- Batch 8, C1/S3, 400 K and 7200 s: purity 0.4336, recovery 0.2415.
- Batch 7, C1/S2, 420 K and 7200 s: purity 0.5929, recovery 0.4724.

These observations make S2 the strongest observed solvent partner for C1, but the 20 K difference between batches 7 and 8 prevents attributing their full difference to solvent.

Catalyst identity also changed the product/byproduct split. Under 420 K, 7200 s conditions, C2/S1 in batch 9 was highly unselective, while C3/S2 in batch 10 gave conversion 0.7692, selectivity 0.4073, purity 0.4842, and recovery 0.3166. C1/S2 remained better than C3/S2 on both conversion and target recovery. Because a complete crossed catalyst-by-solvent design was not run, I cannot state that C1 is universally best; the supported conclusion is narrower: C1/S2 was the best tested reaction pair.

The early diagonal screen also showed that anonymous indices have no meaningful ordinal interpretation:

- Batch 2, C1/S1 at 360 K: final recovery 0.1134, purity 0.4277.
- Batch 3, C2/S2 at 390 K: recovery 0.0762, purity 0.2536.
- Batch 4, C3/S3 at 330 K: recovery 0.0347, purity 0.3442.

Since temperature varied simultaneously, these results are screening evidence, not clean catalyst comparisons.

### Added component

Batch 5 included 0.04 mol of component 0 in addition to the nominal reagent, then used C0/S1 at 350 K for 3600 s. Its pre-workup HPLC values were conversion 0.3225, selectivity 0.3436, purity 0.3376, and recovery 0.1041. The final organic workup gave purity 0.5402 but recovery only 0.0183. There is no matched C0/S1 control, so the component's chemical effect is unidentifiable. Operationally, it was important because its charge drew from the same campaign reagent stock, ultimately leaving no substantive limiting reagent for batch 12. The component should therefore not be assumed to be an independent co-reactant stock.

## Extraction and purification mechanism

For a phase pair, a plausible equilibrium description is

D_P = [P]_organic/[P]_aqueous,
D_I = [I]_organic/[I]_aqueous,

with the fraction of target transferred to the organic phase approximated by

F_P,org = D_P V_org/(D_P V_org + V_aq).

Impurities obey an analogous expression. Organic extraction improves purity only when the retained-phase target fraction is sufficiently larger than the corresponding impurity fraction. Recovery after workup can be represented as

recovery ≈ reaction target yield × F_P,retained × (1-wash loss) × (1-handling loss),

and final purity as retained target divided by retained target plus retained impurities and other solutes.

Batch 11 provides the clearest partitioning evidence. Before workup, the C1/S2 reaction had HPLC conversion 0.8958, purity 0.6067, and recovery 0.4617. X2 extraction followed by retention of the organic phase produced final purity 0.6131 and recovery 0.2172. Recovery therefore fell to roughly 47% of the pre-workup value, while purity changed very little. The simplest explanation is that X2 transferred target and major impurities with similar effective partition fractions. It concentrated neither component selectively enough to solve the purity constraint.

Batch 1 showed a different pattern. C0/S0 at 360 K for 1800 s had pre-workup HPLC purity 0.3818 and recovery 0.0582. X0 extraction, organic-phase retention, washing, drying, and concentration yielded final purity 0.8227, the only assay above the required 0.80 threshold, but recovery was reported as zero. X0 workup may therefore reject impurities strongly while also losing nearly all target. Because the starting target amount was already small and the final target result was at the zero boundary, batch 1 does not establish a reliable high-purity recovery process.

Batch 5 also used X0 organic extraction and washing. Purity rose from the pre-workup value 0.3376 to 0.5402, but recovery fell from 0.1041 to 0.0183. This supports the interpretation that X0 can enrich the retained organic material in target relative to impurities, but with a severe target-recovery penalty under the tested conditions.

Aqueous retention did not provide purification in the early trials. Batch 2 retained the aqueous phase after X1 extraction and finished at purity 0.4277 and recovery 0.1134; batch 3 used X2 and finished at 0.2536 and 0.0762; batch 4 used X3 and finished at 0.3442 and 0.0347. These results are confounded with three different reactions and do not permit ranking aqueous partition coefficients.

Drying and concentration are best interpreted as solvent-removal operations. They should change volume and concentration more readily than moles of target, although handling losses may be embedded in the simulator. There was no matched comparison isolating either operation, so their individual recovery effects are not identifiable.

## Measurement behavior and anomalous transitions

HPLC and final assay often agreed well when no phase workup intervened. Batch 7 changed only slightly from HPLC conversion/purity/recovery of 0.8906/0.5903/0.4707 to final-assay values of 0.9043/0.5929/0.4724. This supports treating these measurements as noisy views of nearly the same material state. The declared instrumental uncertainties are far smaller than many of the observed inter-batch differences, although process variability was not replicated.

In contrast, batches 1 and 5 showed final conversions near unity after organic workup despite much lower pre-workup HPLC conversions:

- Batch 1: HPLC conversion 0.1106; final-assay conversion 0.9946.
- Batch 5: HPLC conversion 0.3225; final-assay conversion 0.9913.

These jumps should not be interpreted straightforwardly as additional chemical conversion because the materials, selected phase, concentration, and assay context changed. Possible explanations include phase-specific conversion definitions, preferential removal of unreacted reagent, continued reaction during downstream residence despite nominal quenching, or a final-assay normalization that differs from reactor HPLC. The public contract explicitly warns that reaction and downstream metrics need not assay the same material. Consequently, conversion comparisons across a phase-selection boundary are less mechanistically reliable than within-stage comparisons.

The same caution applies to selectivity. Batch 11 moved from HPLC selectivity 0.4923 to final 0.2277 after selecting the organic phase, even while purity stayed near 0.61. This indicates that assay selectivity is not simply synonymous with selected-phase purity.

## How the explanation changed during the campaign

The first experiment suggested that an organic X0 workup could cross the purity threshold, because batch 1 reached purity 0.8227. Its zero recovery immediately qualified that hypothesis: purity alone could be obtained by discarding essentially all target.

Batches 2–4 shifted attention toward reaction optimization. They showed low-to-moderate conversion and poor final recovery across several diagonal catalyst/solvent choices. Batch 5 tested an added component but did not establish a benefit and exposed the shared-stock coupling.

Batches 6–10 established the main reaction-level explanation. Higher severity raised conversion, while catalyst–solvent pairing controlled whether that conversion became target or byproduct. Batch 7 identified C1/S2 as the strongest tested reaction condition, whereas batch 9 demonstrated that high conversion with C2/S1 could still be almost useless because selectivity collapsed.

Batch 11 then tested whether an X2 organic workup could purify the best reaction. It halved recovery without a meaningful purity increase, changing the workup hypothesis from 'organic extraction is generally purifying' to 'partition selectivity is extractant- and mixture-dependent, and X2 is approximately nonselective for the C1/S2 mixture.'

Batch 12 did not constitute a valid chemical experiment. The reagent stock had been consumed, chiefly because batch 5's component charge used the same stock. Its zero HPLC response and subsequent discard reflect absent viable reactant, not evidence about C1/S2 or X0 workup.

## Scope and limitations

The conclusions apply only to the anonymous benchmark materials, charge sizes, temperature range, and batch operations tested. Material indices are categorical labels, not real chemical identities.

No condition was replicated. Thus stochastic process variation cannot be distinguished from small condition effects. Most comparisons changed multiple variables, particularly catalyst, solvent, temperature, extractant, and retained phase. Exact rate constants, activation energies, reaction orders, equilibrium partition coefficients, and degradation constants are therefore unidentifiable.

The catalyst amount was normally 0.005 mol and reagent charge normally 0.04 mol, so catalyst loading was not independently varied. Solvent volume was generally 0.04 L. Mixing and settling were not systematically varied, so the campaign cannot distinguish equilibrium partitioning from mass-transfer limitations. Wash intensity was also not studied systematically.

No direct pH, water content, species concentration, or molecular identity was observed. Purity, selectivity, and conversion are synthetic instrument outputs, and the hidden species-to-signal mapping is unavailable. The proposed differential equations and partition equations are mechanistic conjectures consistent with the observations, not uniquely fitted laws.

## Plausible alternative explanations

An alternative to true catalyst–solvent chemical interaction is that solvents change measurement response or phase availability. However, the large differences in final unworked-up recovery, especially batch 7 versus batch 9, favor a real process-level effect even if its molecular origin is unknown.

The extraction losses could arise from incomplete equilibrium, emulsion/settling losses, or selection bookkeeping rather than equilibrium partition coefficients alone. Since only one mixing and settling protocol was used for most worked-up batches, these alternatives cannot be separated.

The near-unity final conversion in batches 1 and 5 could reflect ongoing chemistry during the relatively long workup rather than assay normalization. Quenching nominally occurred, so this would imply incomplete quench; there was no time-course measurement after quenching to test that possibility.

Finally, apparent purification may partly reflect removal of unreacted reagent rather than selective retention of product over byproduct. That would raise reported purity or conversion while still losing target, which is compatible with batch 1.

## Overall account

The most defensible model is a kinetically accelerated but selectivity-limited reaction followed by phase partitioning that can trade recovery for purity. C1/S2 at 420 K for 7200 s was the best tested reaction state, with approximately 0.47 recovery but only 0.59 purity. X2 organic extraction of that mixture was essentially nonselective and reduced recovery to 0.217 without solving purity. X0 workup showed stronger apparent impurity rejection, but the tested instances suffered major or complete target loss. Hence the campaign found no practically successful process satisfying both substantial recovery and purity at least 0.80. Batch 1 was selected only because it was the sole formally purity-feasible completed assay; its zero measured recovery makes that selection a constraint-driven boundary result rather than evidence of a useful operating process.

payload.rationale: The closest campaign evidence is the C1/S2 system. At 420 K and 7200 s, batch 7 gave final purity 0.593 and recovery 0.472 without extraction. Batch 11 used the same reaction followed by X2 organic extraction and gave purity 0.613 and recovery 0.217, indicating that X2 transferred roughly half the target while providing little intrinsic purification at its tested phase ratio. I extrapolated to 400 K with lower conversion and treated the 0.97 transfer as a proportional recovery loss with negligible purity effect. Q01–Q06 use only 0.00025 mol catalyst with 0.04 mol reagent, one twentieth of the campaign catalyst/reagent ratio, so their predicted recoveries are low; longer heating raises Q02 relative to Q01. X0 is predicted to increase purity but lose more target, based on batches 1 and 5, hence Q03 has higher purity and lower recovery than the matched X2 recipe Q04. For X2, increasing organic volume raises recovery but can admit more impurity, producing the Q05–Q06 tradeoff. Q07–Q12 use 0.00025 mol catalyst with only 0.002 mol reagent, restoring the campaign catalyst/reagent ratio. Their estimates are therefore much higher than Q01–Q06, but their intervals are wide because the campaign did not directly test this dilute charge and conversion could depend on absolute catalyst concentration rather than loading alone. Washing is predicted to raise purity while modestly lowering recovery; two staged washes in Q10 should be somewhat more effective and lossy than one equal-total wash in Q09. Concentration removes solvent rather than specified solute, so Q11 and Q12 have essentially equal mole-based purity and recovery predictions. The broad intervals incorporate uncertain temperature kinetics, dilution effects, partition coefficients, wash losses, and final-assay variability.

payload.report:
1. No task-specific instance prior or nominal material-property dossier was supplied; the anonymous indices carried no stated chemical ordering. My main self-developed reaction law—conversion increasing with effective catalyst activity, temperature, and time, while catalyst–solvent pairing separately controls selectivity—was qualitatively supported but not quantitatively identified. Batch 7 (C1/S2, 420 K, 7200 s) gave conversion 0.904, selectivity 0.518, and recovery 0.472, while batch 9 reached high conversion, 0.818, with C2/S1 but only 0.083 selectivity and 0.080 recovery. This changed my judgment from treating conversion as a useful primary objective to treating conversion and selectivity as distinct coupled responses. The approximate unworked-up law recovery ≈ conversion × selectivity was supported by batches 6 and 7. A general claim that organic extraction improves purity while retaining product was contradicted: batch 11 changed purity only from 0.607 before X2 workup to 0.613 finally, while recovery fell from 0.462 to 0.217. X0 showed possible purification in batches 1 and 5, but with severe target loss; batch 1 reached purity 0.823 with zero reported recovery. Exact Arrhenius kinetics, reaction orders, catalyst-loading dependence, distribution coefficients, wash-stage independence, and concentration-operation neutrality remained untested or only weakly tested. The large HPLC-to-final conversion jumps in batches 1 and 5 also contradicted any assumption that reactor and post-workup conversion values were directly interchangeable.

2. I would run one matched, unworked-up C1/S2 experiment at 420 K for 7200 s using 0.002 mol reagent, 0.00025 mol catalyst, and 0.040 L solvent, followed by quench, HPLC, termination, and final assay. This preserves the 0.125 catalyst/reagent ratio of batch 7 while lowering both reagent and catalyst concentrations twentyfold. My prediction set implicitly leaned toward catalyst/reagent ratio being important, whereas the main alternative is that fractional conversion depends strongly on absolute catalyst concentration or bimolecular concentration terms. Conversion, selectivity, and recovery near batch 7 values would support the loading-ratio explanation and strengthen Q07–Q12. Much lower conversion with similar selectivity would support an absolute-concentration kinetic model and require sharply lowering their recovery predictions. Lower conversion plus altered selectivity would indicate additional solvent-concentration or speciation coupling, undermining both simple models. Replicate uncertainty would remain, but this single matched contrast would address the largest extrapolation directly.

3. I did not use the raw spectral traces, peak assignments, or detailed characterization artifacts; the processed estimates were sufficient for the campaign decisions but discarded potentially useful diagnostics about detection limits and signal overlap. Cost, native score, most risk trajectories, control-configuration metadata, and failed-operation readouts were also not used as chemical evidence. Batch 12 was correctly excluded from mechanism inference because it lacked a substantive reagent charge. Sampling losses were treated as negligible rather than estimated. No replicates were collected, and the campaign lacked a complete catalyst-by-solvent factorial design or matched extraction controls.

The least reliable predictions are Q07–Q12 because their 0.002 mol reagent charge and dilute absolute catalyst concentration were never tested, even though their catalyst/reagent ratio matched the campaign. Q01–Q06 also extrapolate twentyfold below the tested catalyst loading. Q03 is especially uncertain because X0 evidence came only from confounded batches 1 and 5. The staged-wash effect in Q10 and the claimed near-equivalence of Q11 and Q12 are weak because wash staging and concentration were not isolated experimentally.

The sealed recommendation of batch 1 is reliable only as a literal constraint decision: it was the sole completed assay with purity at least 0.80. It is not a reliable practical recommendation because its measured recovery was zero. Batch 7 is the strongest reaction recommendation but violates the purity requirement.

The assigned goal materially affected evidence collection. It motivated organic extraction, phase selection, washing, drying, and concentration tests rather than a purely kinetic campaign, and it forced final selection by the purity threshold rather than native score or maximum recovery. There was no inherent conflict in the goal, but execution created one: the exploratory component charge in batch 5 consumed shared reagent stock, preventing a valid twelfth assay. More disciplined stock accounting, replication of batch 7, and a matched X0/X2 workup comparison would have produced stronger evidence.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 1 is the only completed batch whose final assay met the mandatory purity threshold (purity 0.8227). Its recovery was reported as zero, so this is a strict constraint-feasible selection rather than a practically successful process; higher-recovery batch 7 was excluded because purity was only 0.5929.
